description.narrative: As an overview, the scoping study revealed the following key findings: 1. Biodiversity credits are being developed across Africa to access private finance for sustainable long-term conservation and restoration by private, community and government entities. 2. The biodiversity credit developers interviewed for this study tend to design products predicated on measures spanning three characteristics: territorial expanse, ecosystem robustness, and individual keystone or iconic species. 3. In contrast to carbon credits, biodiversity credits proffer unique opportunities to invest in a diverse array of African landscapes, ecosystems, and species, extending beyond those traditionally employed to demonstrate carbon sequestration (as evinced by the projects mapped herein). 4. Nonetheless, African biodiversity credits have largely drawn upon the experiences of carbon markets to date, exhibiting a co-dependency in price discovery, and potentially demand. Most developers are designing financial models that entail stacking, stapling, and bundling biodiversity credits with carbon credits until demand for the former gains traction. The mapping demonstrates that the hubs of activity in biodiversity credit markets, particularly concentrated in Southern and East Africa, coincide with those of carbon markets on the continent. 5. Debates around using biodiversity credits for offsetting remain unsettled locally and globally. Many see offsetting requirements as crucial for scaling private investment and driving demand, but concerns exist around equivalence and integrity. Clear regulation and oversight embedded in financial reporting should be adopted with any offsetting approach. 6. Numerous project developers frequently collaborate with international conservation, philanthropic, and academic entities, actively shaping the market through participation in international methodology pilots and biocredit forums. 7. New nature-focused tech is emerging to manage projects, quantify impacts and offer data aggregation, transparency and accessibility functions, including for smallholders/CSOs. 8. There is no active biodiversity credits market yet in Africa at national/regional levels. Innovative projects and supply collaborations exist but few committed buyers. This is likely because projects need years to demonstrate impact, and currently lack strong policy incentives driving demand. 9. Emerging shifts are inclining toward biodiversity-specific standards, including the Society for Ecological Restoration and Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) Global Biodiversity Standard. Additionally, numerous methodologies are under development across African projects, including uniquely African methodologies such as ValueNature's, as well as international methodologies piloting with African projects, namely those of Plan Vivo and Verra. 10. Indigenous and local communities involved in biodiversity credit projects face severe challenges related to financial and capacity constraints, alongside contested land ownership and human rights issues. Many project developers consulted in this study possess years of experience engaging and working with local communities and are working to integrate community expertise and foster local ownership into the development of biodiversity credit projects in novel ways. 11. At the time of publication, no specific biodiversity credits policy/regulation yet exists nationally/regionally. This enables innovation but creates risks around demand, governance of impacts/benefits, and quality control, akin to carbon markets. Policymakers are largely unaware of these instruments but are interested to learn more.

Global conversations on nature markets, specifically bio-credits, have advanced in recent years. However, the lack of strong representation from Africa has risked undermining these efforts and continuing to disadvantage the continent in the nature, climate, and development discourse. We have seen a fragmentation of initiatives and efforts across the African continent, necessitating an effort to bring together relevant stakeholders with a market-shaping approach.
To address this, a scoping study was conducted to outline how best to drive a coordinated and systemic approach across Africa in transforming key value chains and economies that are dependent on nature. Given the current situation and the fact that no extensive study on bio-credits in Africa had been previously undertaken, the urgent need to carry out a scoping assessment was identified, to better understand Africa's bio-credits space and map out a roadmap towards convening a Pan-African voice and effort that leverages nature as a pathway to green development.
The scoping exercise sought to better understand who was doing what across the continent, what the gaps were, and how Africa (sovereign states, regions, local communities, and Indigenous peoples) could position itself to strategically take leadership in the nature markets space globally. At the core of this was also the determination of how Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs), as the primary nature custodians, could drive and benefit from this opportunity.
The initial findings of the scoping exercise were launched at Climate COP28, hosted by the Government of the UAE in December 2023. The outcomes represent an attempt to achieve a coordinated and streamlined engagement of Africa in the bio-credits market, both locally and globally. Policy recommendations have also been put forth in an attempt to address the previous fragmentation and strengthening Africa's voice and representation with an aim of better positioning the continent to leverage nature as a pathway to sustainable development and climate action.
Key stakeholders included but were not limited to the following: 1. IPLCs 2. Government Representatives 3. Project developers 4. Conservation organisations 5. Private Sector 6. Policy makers

The project involved conducting a comprehensive scoping study to understand the current state of biodiversity credits across Africa. Its key objectives were to: 1. Explore the feasibility of a coordinated approach to biodiversity credit development in Africa. 2. Recommend key interventions to scale nature finance on the continent. 3. Ensure African perspectives were incorporated into global discussions on biodiversity credits.
Importantly, this study was designed to feed directly into the work of the International Advisory Panel on Biocredits (IAPB) – funnel flow. By capturing the unique African context and perspectives, the study aimed to ensure that Africa's voice would be heard and considered in shaping global biodiversity credit markets. This aligns with the growing body of work on biocredits, following initiatives by France and the UK, positioning Africa as an active participant in this emerging field.
Key Activities included: 1. Conducting interviews with over 80 stakeholders across the nature finance ecosystem. 2. Performing extensive literature reviews on biodiversity credits and related topics. 3. Attending and organizing events to socialize findings and gather feedback. 4. Producing a comprehensive scoping report with actionable recommendations. 5. Mapping over 30 biodiversity credit projects across Africa, showcasing the diversity of approaches and innovations.
The study highlighted Africa's potential to become a "nature economy superpower" by leveraging its vast natural capital through biodiversity credits. It emphasized the importance of ensuring equitable outcomes and empowering Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs) in the process.
This study was critical in connecting Africa’s perspectives, realities and contributions to the global IAPB work. This is because the project aimed to: a.) Ensure African perspectives influence global standards and practices for biodiversity credits. b.) Highlight unique African innovations and approaches that could inform global market development. c.) Address potential risks and challenges specific to the African context in global policy discussions. d.) Position African stakeholders as key players in shaping the future of biodiversity finance.
This work was particularly timely and crucial as it coincided with growing international interest in biodiversity credits as a tool for conservation finance. By proactively engaging in this space, the study aimed to prevent the inequalities and challenges seen in carbon credit markets from being replicated in biodiversity markets.

sector.narrative:
Nature markets are a sub-set of the economy where nature is specifically traded and valued. This includes large markets such as agricultural commodities and emerging markets like biodiversity credits that reflect the growing economic value of nature.
If markets can be shaped to treat nature as a regenerative asset, they can play an important role in addressing nature loss, climate change, equality and food security issues.
Our work on shaping nature markets aims to place nature and equity at the centre of how we build and run businesses, markets and economies.

tag.narrative: By exploring the potential of bio-credits markets, the study supports the transition towards more sustainable patterns of production and consumption in Africa. It helps to highlight the true value of natural resources and ecosystem services, promoting their efficient use and conservation. The study's focus on transforming key value chains and economies dependent on nature aligns directly with SDG 12's emphasis on sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources. By mapping out how Africa can take leadership in nature markets, the study encourages the development of sustainable business practices and market mechanisms that internalize environmental costs.

The scoping study on bio-credits in Africa significantly contributes to the achievement of SDG. By mapping the bio-credits landscape across the continent and identifying key stakeholders, gaps, and opportunities, the study lays the groundwork for more effective conservation and sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems. It highlights the potential of bio-credits as an innovative financial mechanism to value and protect biodiversity, forests, and other land resources. By emphasizing the role of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs) as primary nature custodians, the study promotes their inclusion in decision-making processes and benefit-sharing schemes, aligning with SDG 15's targets on fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. Furthermore, by positioning Africa to take leadership in the nature markets space globally, the study supports the integration of ecosystem and biodiversity values into national and local planning, poverty reduction strategies, and accounts, as called for in SDG 15. Ultimately, this work contributes to halting biodiversity loss, promoting sustainable land management, and enhancing Africa's capacity to leverage its natural capital for sustainable development, all key components of SDG 15.

description.narrative:
This report delves into the transformative potential of nature credit instruments to catalyse private investment in African conservation and restoration efforts. It provides key insights, offering a panoramic view of the continent's burgeoning biodiversity credit landscape. Our analysis is grounded in extensive research, including in-depth interviews with over 80 industry stakeholders, whose invaluable contributions we gratefully acknowledge. The study also considers global market trends, ensuring a contextualized understanding of Africa's position in the international nature finance arena. This thorough exploration of the biocredit markets, coupled with strategic stakeholder engagement, was conducted in collaboration with Advancing Green and made possible through the generous support of FSD Africa.
The recommended interventions aim to establish market trust, promote equitable development, and ensure fair compensation in Africa’s biodiversity credit markets. The six principles with corresponding interventions to achieve them are: 1. Quality of biodiversity credits; 2. Market incentives and disincentives; 3. Equitable market access; 4. Fair price for both nature-rich countries and nature’s stewards, local communities and developers; 5. Establishing regulations for transparency and efficient biocredit trading; and 6. Building stakeholder voices into the core market design.
